SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p289/r3.claim: The past akhkhartani indicates that the fatal loss has already happened; a present verb could suggest the matter has not yet occurred and there is still time.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p290/r1.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p290/r1.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p290/r1.claim: The dying person asks for a specifically near, short reprieve to make up for time wasted heedlessly, rather than an unspecified term that might be long or short.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p290/r2.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p290/r2.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p290/r2.claim: The rapid fa, omitted vocative ya, and insistent lawla compress the appeal and signal the speaker's terror and urgency to gain a little time.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p290/r3.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p290/r3.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p290/r3.claim: Iblis seeks delay to mislead Adam's descendants, not for personal benefit or to avert harm; the dying person seeks delay for his own salvation.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p291/r1.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p291/r1.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p291/r1.claim: The sincere request for the speaker's own benefit states the pronoun, while Iblis's request, which serves no personal interest, omits it.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p291/r2.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p291/r2.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p291/r2.claim: Iblis's wording is an indirect request embedded in an oath-condition, whereas lawla is an explicit request; the pronoun difference mirrors that contrast.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p291/r3.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p291/r3.speaker: جمهور السبعة
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p291/r3.claim: The majority of the Seven readers recite أكن in the jussive.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p291/r4.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p291/r4.speaker: الزمخشري
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p291/r4.claim: Al-Zamakhshari explains the jussive أكن by its coordination with the syntactic position of فأصدق, as though the meaning were conditional.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p291/r5.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p291/r5.speaker: ابن عطية
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p291/r5.claim: Ibn Atiyya analyzes أكن as coordinated with the underlying position, estimating إن تؤخرني أصدق وأكن.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p292/r1.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p292/r1.speaker: معاني النحو
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p292/r1.claim: Maʿani al-Nahw explains the mixed inflection as combining causal purpose in فأصدق with a conditional response to the request in وأكن, illustrated by parallel request and causal examples.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p293/r1.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p293/r1.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p293/r1.claim: Righteousness matters more than almsgiving for salvation: a person may lack anything to give, while the deceased in al-Muʾminun asks to return to do good deeds; righteousness is framed as a binding condition and charity as a lesser cause.

STUDYQURAN:63:10/r1.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:63:10/r1.speaker: Q
STUDYQURAN:63:10/r1.claim: These verses indicate that zakāh should be paid promptly and obligatory religious duties should not be delayed.

STUDYQURAN:63:10/r2.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:63:10/r2.speaker: Ibn ʿAbbās
STUDYQURAN:63:10/r2.claim: At death, anyone who fell short in paying zakāh will ask to return to this world, apparently to make up the missed payment.

STUDYQURAN:63:10/r4.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:63:10/r4.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:63:10/r4.claim: The warning follows the sūrah’s theme of hypocrisy: although sincere repentance is possible before death, one should not deliberately wait until death to repent.
